title: Progressive spastic weakness with a discordant prior label
opening: A patient has bilateral leg weakness and spastic paraplegia, reduced pinprick sensation below T3–T4 and occasional urinary incontinence over two years, with worsening during the last year. Earlier clinicians labelled the illness multiple sclerosis or myelitis.
initial_facts:
A patient has bilateral leg weakness and spastic paraplegia, reduced pinprick sensation below T3–T4 and occasional urinary incontinence over two years, with worsening during the last year. Earlier clinicians labelled the illness multiple sclerosis or myelitis.
Brain imaging shows punctate-to-patchy white-matter abnormalities, with sparing of the corpus callosum, cerebellum and brainstem. Spinal imaging shows a symmetric, long-segment ring-like white-matter pattern, relatively sparing central grey matter. CSF cellularity and IgG index are normal, and oligoclonal bands are negative. Age, family history and genetic results are not supplied.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Write a one-sentence clinical problem representation, up to three prioritised diagnostic categories and the next investigations that would distinguish them. Explain how the imaging and CSF affect, but do not by themselves settle, the earlier diagnosis. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: The source later associates the syndrome with PLAAT4 variants using family/genetic and functional work. Those results, the gene name and cohort summary were not supplied. The reported absence of enhancement in the paper concerns P2, not an established P1 finding.
reference: Integrate a progressive spinal-predominant syndrome and the atypical imaging rather than accepting the prior label automatically. An acquired inflammatory cause and inherited/metabolic white-matter disease are defensible categories to discuss; negative oligoclonal bands alone do not establish or exclude a diagnosis. Family history and targeted genetic/other specialist investigation can be proposed without naming the hidden gene. Keep the patient-specific evidence separate from group summaries; age and enhancement status remain unreported.

source_location: Results > Identification of a Novel Spinal Predominant Leukoencephalopathy: P1 paragraph and P1/P2 CSF paragraph.

title: Tissue target engagement and clinical benefit
source_patient: Eight autopsy tissue donors; no synthetic individual
opening: This is an autopsy-tissue series, not an individual diagnostic vignette. Eight deceased people with SOD1-associated ALS had received intrathecal tofersen. Tissue concentrations were examined against dosing histories and pharmacokinetic predictions.
initial_facts:
This is an autopsy-tissue series, not an individual diagnostic vignette. Eight deceased people with SOD1-associated ALS had received intrathecal tofersen. Tissue concentrations were examined against dosing histories and pharmacokinetic predictions.
In three recently treated donors, lumbar spinal-cord SOD1 mRNA/protein reductions were reported in the range 45%–84%, relative to tofersen-naive tissue samples. The size and matching of that comparison cohort are not specified in this packet. Residual motor neurons contained drug-related signal; misfolded SOD1 inclusions remained detectable. This packet supplies no randomised clinical comparison, patient-level functional trajectory or survival estimate.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Summarise what these measurements support about drug delivery and target engagement, and what they cannot establish about clinical improvement or survival. Distinguish measured findings, mechanistic interpretation and any further evidence needed for a clinical-effect claim. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: The paper also describes meningeal/perivascular infiltrates and other mechanistic findings. They are not supplied here and are not required. Other clinical trials discussed in the source are outside this packet.
reference: The eight-donor study and three-donor reduction subset must remain distinct. Tissue distribution and reduced target measures support biological target engagement in sampled tissue. They do not by themselves estimate clinical benefit, comparative survival, universal response or an individual treatment recommendation. The 45%–84% range is not a clinical response rate or an effect in all eight donors. Lack of a supplied functional comparison should be acknowledged without dismissing the measured tissue results.
article_title: Antisense Oligonucleotide Tofersen Distribution in the Central Nervous System of SOD1-ALS Autopsy Tissue Donors
source_location: Abstract > Design / Main Outcomes / Results; main Methods and Results on tissue concentrations and SOD1 measurements.

title: Recovery before and after rescue immunotherapy
opening: A retrospective multicentre series records 18 treated attacks in 17 people with MOGAD or AQP4-positive NMOSD. IL-6 receptor blockade began within one month of attack nadir. Thirteen attacks were treated as acute escalation after inadequate earlier therapy; five represented early initiation of maintenance treatment.
initial_facts:
A retrospective multicentre series records 18 treated attacks in 17 people with MOGAD or AQP4-positive NMOSD. IL-6 receptor blockade began within one month of attack nadir. Thirteen attacks were treated as acute escalation after inadequate earlier therapy; five represented early initiation of maintenance treatment.
The authors report an EDSS improvement before IL-6 blockade, from a nadir median of 5.0 to a pre-blockade median of 3.5 (P=.001), and a further decrease to 2.0 at three months (P=.03 versus pre-blockade). These are the reported comparison summaries; the packet does not establish the participant subset for every paired comparison. There is no concurrent untreated control group. Earlier corticosteroids/plasma exchange and spontaneous recovery can affect the course.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Explain what the sequence supports and what it leaves unresolved about an acute rescue effect. Address attacks versus patients, the two treatment intentions, the improvement already present before blockade, and why the reported P values do not alone identify a causal effect. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: The source reports visual-acuity outcomes, infections and other details that are not supplied. No patient-specific management decision or hidden final diagnosis is required.
reference: Do not count 18 attacks as 18 independent patients. Escalation and early-maintenance intentions differ. Improvement preceding blockade must not be attributed to blockade. Subsequent change is an association in a selected uncontrolled series, with prior therapy, natural recovery and subset uncertainty. Statistical significance is not a randomised causal contrast. Do not convert changes in an ordinal EDSS median into a validated percentage recovery.
article_title: IL-6 Receptor Blockade as Rescue Therapy in Acute Attacks of MOGAD and AQP4+NMOSD
source_location: Methods; Results paragraphs on 18 attacks / 17 patients, escalation versus maintenance intent, and pre/post-treatment EDSS.
review_questions: Are the two treatment-intent groups sufficiently distinct to require separate interpretation?

title: Respiratory illness after long-term B-cell depletion
opening: A man in his early forties with multiple sclerosis has received ocrelizumab for 10.6 years, with 23 infusions. New respiratory illness develops five weeks after his last infusion. His pre-symptom IgG is 422 mg/dL.
initial_facts:
A man in his early forties with multiple sclerosis has received ocrelizumab for 10.6 years, with 23 infusions. New respiratory illness develops five weeks after his last infusion. His pre-symptom IgG is 422 mg/dL.
HRCT shows ground-glass change with peripheral/migratory consolidation. BAL has 69.7% lymphocytes, 25% macrophages, 4% neutrophils and 1.3% eosinophils. SARS-CoV-2 testing is negative. Smoking history is negative. Cryobiopsy findings, other microbiological results, treatment response and subsequent drug decisions are not available in this packet. Exact respiratory symptoms are not allocated to this patient in the source table.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Give a one-sentence problem representation and a short assessment of inflammatory/drug-related and infectious explanations. State what must still be checked before making a causal attribution or a treatment decision. Do not assume that many years of stable exposure excludes a treatment-related complication. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: Patient 1 later had cryobiopsy support, clinical recovery and resumed ocrelizumab. The series-wide mean restart delay is not this patient’s documented delay. Other patients’ fatal outcomes are not this patient’s outcome.
reference: Use the patient-specific timing, immune context, imaging and BAL without adding all symptoms listed for the group. Negative SARS-CoV-2 does not exclude every infection. The pattern can support an organising/inflammatory lung process, while a drug-specific causal conclusion remains provisional. Proportionate pulmonary/neurology assessment, remaining microbiology and relevant tissue evidence can be discussed. Do not claim that IgG decline proves the mechanism or prescribe a steroid regimen from this packet.

title: Progressive language-led impairment after earlier haemorrhage
source_patient: Detailed index patient, decision point around age 55
opening: A man first developed difficulty organising appointments at age 47. At 49 he had a right parieto-occipital intracerebral haemorrhage, then attributed to hypertension; he recovered physically but required a live-in carer.
initial_facts:
A man first developed difficulty organising appointments at age 47. At 49 he had a right parieto-occipital intracerebral haemorrhage, then attributed to hypertension; he recovered physically but required a live-in carer.
By 54, disorientation and loss of recent-event recall had progressed. At approximately 55, speech remained fluent and grammatical, but word retrieval and sentence repetition were markedly impaired; comprehension was relatively preserved. Navigation and dressing also became difficult. He received cadaveric pituitary-derived growth hormone during childhood, including 1974–1985. Current brain imaging, CSF biomarkers, genetic results and pathology are not supplied.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Provide a one-sentence problem representation, a short differential for the progressive cognitive/language syndrome and the next evidence needed to distinguish causes. Preserve the distinction between a previous vascular event, the progressive syndrome and a possible exposure-related hypothesis. Do not claim a pathology-confirmed diagnosis. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: At 56 the patient had advanced disability and imaging abnormalities; later testing and postmortem examination supported high-level Alzheimer-type change with severe cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Those later results and the three other patients’ findings were withheld.
reference: Progressive language, cognitive and functional change should not be explained solely by a remote stroke without qualification. Fluent language, impaired repetition and atypical features warrant careful phenotype description rather than a rigid PPA subtype. The childhood exposure is relevant to specialist assessment but does not alone establish the cause in this packet. Neurodegenerative, vascular/mixed and exposure-associated possibilities may be discussed. Pathology, genetic results and current imaging are not established in this packet.
article_title: High-Level Alzheimer Disease Neuropathological Change Following Iatrogenic Exposure
source_location: Results: first three clinical-history paragraphs; later NPC assessment and postmortem sections excluded from input.
review_questions: What phenotype and differential are defensible at this earlier decision point?
How much diagnostic commitment to an exposure-related process is justified before imaging, biomarkers or pathology?

title: Explaining a staged infant treatment plan
opening: Your infant son was diagnosed on day 24 through newborn screening and confirmatory testing with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type II. An IDS variant and undetectable relevant enzyme activity were found.
initial_facts:
Your infant son was diagnosed on day 24 through newborn screening and confirmatory testing with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type II. An IDS variant and undetectable relevant enzyme activity were found.
Intravenous enzyme replacement began at two months, and enzyme delivery into the brain’s fluid spaces began at three months. The specialist team is preparing a cord-blood transplant at nine months, after growth and donor coordination. The paper’s rationale is that blood-delivered treatment and transplant do not address brain involvement equally well in type II disease. Transplant outcomes, later development and complications are not yet available at this task’s decision point.
task: Audience: the infant’s parents. Use 220–280 words in plain English. Explain to the parents why the team is considering more than one treatment route, why treatment is staged, and what the plan cannot guarantee. Describe the broad risks and questions to discuss with the specialist team in accessible language. Do not give procedural instructions or promise a particular developmental outcome. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: Infant 3 later had mild sinusoidal obstruction, a SARS-CoV-2 infection, no acute GVHD, and resumed brain-directed enzyme treatment on day 47. Follow-up outcomes, including developmental quotient, were not supplied. The prompt is a retrospective pretransplant adaptation, not a claim that all infants share these outcomes.
reference: Explain the missing-enzyme problem and the different access of systemic versus brain-directed treatment without implying identical effects in every mucopolysaccharidosis subtype. The stated growth/donor-coordination interval can be explained without inventing a universal optimal transplant age. Acknowledge transplant/procedure risks and uncertain long-term development; do not assume transplant outcomes or later development. Keep jargon explained and avoid a personalised guarantee or instructions to change treatment.
article_title: Newborn Screening and Early Cord Blood Transplant for Mucopolysaccharidosis
source_location: Table 1 patient ID 3; Methods and Results on enzyme replacement timing and the pre-CBT treatment pathway. Later Table 2 outcomes hidden.
review_questions: Is the distinction between systemic, brain-directed and transplant treatment appropriate for a parent explanation?
Which risks and qualifications must be included, and how should original D7b audience anchors be applied?

title: Response denominators and a supportive-treatment claim
opening: A retrospective uncontrolled series treated 33 people with chemotherapy- or radiation-associated skin toxicity using high-dose oral vitamin D. Thirty also received concurrent supportive therapy.
initial_facts:
A retrospective uncontrolled series treated 33 people with chemotherapy- or radiation-associated skin toxicity using high-dose oral vitamin D. Thirty also received concurrent supportive therapy.
During the reported 10-day interval, 26 of 30 people with symptom data reported relief. Anticancer treatment continued without interruption in 24 of all 33. No treatment-related adverse events were reported. Post-treatment laboratory information was inconsistently available; post-treatment vitamin D levels were measured in 13. The packet supplies neither an untreated group nor patient-level pairing for every outcome.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Report the symptom-relief and uninterrupted-treatment percentages with their correct denominators. Explain what the results support about feasibility and observed improvement, and the limits of claims that vitamin D caused recovery or is generally safe. Do not substitute the full cohort denominator for a measured-outcome denominator. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: Other source analyses, erythema scores and mechanisms were not supplied and are not required. The source’s headline and abstract vary in how they describe 26 responders; this task prospectively uses the explicit Results denominator of 30.
reference: Symptom relief is 26/30, about 86.7%; uninterrupted therapy is 24/33, about 72.7%. The 30 measured people and 33 treated people are different denominators. Concurrent supportive treatments and natural recovery preclude attributing the observed outcome solely to vitamin D. No reported adverse events with incomplete follow-up is not proof of zero risk or universal safety. Do not equate no report with systematically verified absence in every patient.
article_title: High-Dose Oral Vitamin D for Toxic Effects of the Skin Associated With Chemotherapy and Radiation
source_location: Results main-text paragraphs on 33 treated patients, concurrent supportive therapy, 26/30 symptomatic relief, calcium follow-up and 24/33 continuation.
review_questions: What safety statement is proportionate to these follow-up data?
Do high grades correctly reward exact denominators and restrained causal conclusions rather than demanding stronger evidence be generated?

title: Clinical shrinkage versus pathological response
opening: A prospective uncontrolled series enrolled 15 people with advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck awaiting surgery. All received neoadjuvant capecitabine.
initial_facts:
A prospective uncontrolled series enrolled 15 people with advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck awaiting surgery. All received neoadjuvant capecitabine.
Ten of 15 had clinical tumour reduction. Twelve underwent surgery; five of those twelve had a complete pathological response and seven of twelve were downstaged. Two people with apparent complete clinical lesion resolution chose radiotherapy instead of surgery; another did not proceed to surgery after progression. No grade 3 or higher treatment-related toxicity was reported. There was no comparator group, and follow-up for durability was short.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Give the clinical-reduction, pathological-complete-response and downstaging percentages with their denominators. Explain why clinical disappearance, pathological response and durable cure are different claims. State what can and cannot be concluded about comparative efficacy and safety. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: The source also gives dosing, individual tumour details and later interpretations, which are not supplied or required. No dose recommendation is requested. Recomputed percentages use one decimal place.
reference: Clinical reduction is 10/15 (66.7%); pathological complete response is 5/12 (41.7%) among surgically assessed people, not all 15; downstaging is 7/12 (58.3%). The two non-surgical clinical responders have no surgical pathology confirmation in this packet. No concurrent comparison or adequate long-term follow-up establishes superiority or durable cure. The absence of reported grade 3+ events is not absence of all toxicity or proof of safety for every subgroup.
article_title: Neoadjuvant Capecitabine in Advanced Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck
source_location: Results: clinical tumour reduction paragraph and pathological stage-migration / Ryan regression grade paragraph; limitations paragraph.
review_questions: Which response and safety wording is appropriate for clinical counselling?

title: An individual nonresponse within a high-response series

initial_facts:
An adult with a small periocular cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma has not responded to a trial of intralesional interleukin-2. The referral biopsy established invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Age, sex, full staging, visual symptoms and detailed comorbidities are not supplied.
The treating team cites a single-centre uncontrolled series in which 13 of 16 people had a complete clinical response and only grade 1/2 treatment-related adverse events were observed. This person is an observed nonresponder. Their subsequent treatment and outcome are not given.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Write a one-sentence representation and advise what the team should review next. Explain whether the series-level 81% complete-response figure justifies continuing unchanged treatment for this individual. Preserve uncertainty about stage and risks, and avoid inventing an emergency or prescribing a regimen. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. title: Early severe skin disease with normal glucose
opening: An eight-year-old boy had skin laxity at birth. From about age two, progressive hyperpigmented velvety thickening began in skin folds and became generalised. He has sparse curly hair, numerous skin tags, mild cognitive impairment, developmental delay, enamel erosion and low bone mineral density. No similar skin disorder is reported in the family.
initial_facts:
An eight-year-old boy had skin laxity at birth. From about age two, progressive hyperpigmented velvety thickening began in skin folds and became generalised. He has sparse curly hair, numerous skin tags, mild cognitive impairment, developmental delay, enamel erosion and low bone mineral density. No similar skin disorder is reported in the family.
Glucose status is described as normal. A popliteal skin biopsy shows hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis and acanthosis without an inflammatory infiltrate. Molecular results, chest imaging and treatment response have not been supplied.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Give a one-sentence problem representation and explain why the presentation should not automatically be attributed to insulin resistance. Propose proportionate next genetic/systemic assessment and state what cannot yet be concluded. Do not predict a specific molecular result or diagnose an unreported systemic disorder. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.
decision_point: Assess only the information and task actually supplied at this point.
hidden: The source later identifies a de novo germline EGFR L858R variant in patient 2, with pulmonary nodules found after molecular investigation and improvement during targeted treatment. Patient 3 has a different mosaic distribution; patient 1 has different age, comorbidity and lung pathology.
reference: Integrate early-onset severe generalised skin findings with associated developmental and other features rather than treating normal glucose as proof that no relevant disease exists. A syndromic/genetic assessment and review for systemic involvement are defensible. Negative reported family history does not exclude a de novo disorder. Molecular cause, systemic investigation results and treatment response remain unknown. Keep the supplied individual separate from other patients.
